tagline: From Lincoln’s childhood farms to the brick mansion at Federal Hill.
intro: Old Kentucky Turnpike follows US 31E from the Abraham Lincoln birthplace through Hodgenville to Bardstown, then US 62 and US 150 to My Old Kentucky Home State Park. Kentucky designated this 28.059-mile scenic route on May 24, 1995. The Federal Highway Administration describes the longer Lincoln Heritage Scenic Highway as winding through Kentucky’s knobs, linking Lincoln history, Civil War history, bourbon and religious heritage. LaRue County has low rolling hills, largely cleared for agriculture or development, with wooded drainages in the east.

At Knob Creek, Thomas Lincoln leased land beside the Old Cumberland Trail, now US 31E. A century later, paved roads helped turn Lincoln’s birthplace into a destination for motorists. The Nancy Lincoln Inn and its cabins were built in 1928 to serve those visitors. At Knob Creek, a tavern built in 1933 also catered to the growing Lincoln tourist trade. That building later became a museum and gift shop, which operated until 1998.

Begin at Sinking Spring Farm’s memorial, then continue through Hodgenville, where two bronze Lincolns stand in the square, one a child and one an adult. Knob Creek Farm lies northeast of Hodgenville, near US 31E. At Bardstown, the route finishes at Federal Hill, the former Rowan plantation home that became My Old Kentucky Home.

moments.title: Sinking Spring Farm
moments.text: Fifty-six steps lead to Lincoln’s birthplace memorial, one for each year of his life. Inside is a symbolic cabin whose logs date mostly to the 1840s, rather than the building in which he was born in 1809. Architect John Russell Pope designed the neoclassical memorial; President William Howard Taft dedicated it in November 1911. The cabin proved too large for visitors to circulate easily, so the Lincoln Farm Association reduced it from sixteen by eighteen feet to twelve by seventeen. The memorial also uses groups of sixteen windows and ceiling rosettes to mark Lincoln’s place as the sixteenth president.
moments.notice: The memorial’s 56 entrance steps represent Lincoln’s age at death.

moments.title: Knob Creek Farm
moments.text: Lincoln lived at Knob Creek from age two until age seven, on land his father leased beside the Old Cumberland Trail. The Lincoln family’s cabin was dismantled and its logs reused in a horse stable, later swept away by a flood. The Gollaher Cabin was moved here to represent what their home looked like. The other historic building, Lincoln Tavern, dates to 1933 and began as a dance hall serving the tourist trade. The farm joined the national park in November 2001. The family left for Indiana in December 1816, when Lincoln was almost eight.

moments.title: Federal Hill
moments.text: Federal Hill’s brick exterior rises above a native limestone foundation. John Rowan and Ann Lytle commissioned the mansion, whose main block was completed in 1818 using enslaved labor. Its bricks were fired on the property and laid in Flemish bond. A burial ground for enslaved men, women and children lies southwest of the mansion. The My Old Kentucky Home Commission bought the property in 1922 and gave it to Kentucky after renovation. Dedicated as a historic site in 1923, it passed to the Division of State Parks in 1936. The rear portion, built in 1795, housed the family while the main residence was under construction.
